title: Trump Administration Accuses Yale Medical School of Discriminating Against Asian and White Applicants

body:
The Trump administration has claimed that Yale University's medical school discriminated against Asian American and white applicants in its admissions process, reigniting a fierce national debate over race-conscious policies in higher education. The allegation, advanced by the Department of Justice, asserts that Yale used race as a determining factor in admissions decisions, systematically disadvantaging certain groups.

The claim builds on earlier DOJ investigations into Yale's undergraduate admissions, which had similarly alleged bias against Asian American applicants. Yale has denied the charges, maintaining that its holistic admissions process complies with federal law and serves the goal of training a diverse physician workforce capable of addressing health disparities across communities.

The accusation arrives against the backdrop of the Supreme Court's landmark 2023 ruling that effectively ended race-conscious admissions at American universities. Since that decision, studies have documented a measurable decline in Black and Hispanic enrollment at medical schools, while Asian and white students have seen increased acceptance rates. A joint Yale-NYU study found that acceptance rates for underrepresented groups dropped by as much as 9 percentage points relative to Asian and white applicants in the post-ruling admissions cycle.

For Indian Americans — the largest subset of Asian Americans in many professional graduate programs — the issue cuts both ways. On one hand, the community has long argued that race-conscious admissions unfairly penalised high-achieving Asian applicants. On the other, many Indian American medical professionals and advocacy groups worry that dismantling diversity initiatives could erode progress in addressing health inequities that disproportionately affect minority communities, including South Asians with elevated risks of cardiovascular disease and diabetes.

The case is likely to set a precedent for how medical schools navigate admissions in the post-affirmative-action era, with implications for the pipeline of diverse physicians serving an increasingly multicultural America. For the diaspora, it is a reminder that the politics of race in American institutions remain deeply personal — and far from settled.
author: Diaspora Desk
